items.stem: 40 students are enlisted in MGT 45 and the course title changes. How many rows are written in the flat table, and how many in the split design?

options.text: 40 in the flat table and 1 in the split design.
options.feedback: The flat table stores the title in every enlistment row. The split design stores it once in the courses table.

options.text: 1 in both, because only one title changed.
options.feedback: The flat table has a copy of the title in each of its 40 rows, so all 40 rows must change.

options.text: 40 in both, because the database rewrites every table.
options.feedback: The split design changes one row in the courses table. The enlistments hold only the course id, which did not change.

options.text: 1 in the flat table and 40 in the split design.
options.feedback: The copies are in the flat table, so the flat table needs the 40 writes.

items.stem: A developer renames a course in the flat table but misses 2 of the 40 rows. What does the database do?

options.text: It accepts the change and leaves two titles.
options.feedback: Each row is valid on its own, so no rule is broken. The disagreement stays unnoticed until someone sees it.

options.text: It reports an error naming the 2 rows that were missed.
options.feedback: The database cannot know that two rows should have changed. Nothing is wrong with them individually.

options.text: It updates the 2 missed rows automatically to match.
options.feedback: A database changes only the rows named in the command.

options.text: It rejects the whole change and keeps the old title.
options.feedback: The 38 updated rows are valid, so they are saved.

items.stem: A teammate says the flat table is the better design, because the schedule page then needs no join. What is the best response?

options.text: That is true for reads, but each title change needs one write per enlistment.
options.feedback: The flat design saves a join when reading and costs more when changing. A split design stores each fact once.

options.text: The flat table is always wrong, so the team should never use it.
options.feedback: The flat table is valid and does answer the schedule question without a join. The cost appears when facts change.

options.text: Joins cost nothing, so the split design has no downside at all.
options.feedback: A join does cost something. The cost is usually small compared with the risk of inconsistent copies.

options.text: The split design takes longer to write, so it matters only for large projects.
options.feedback: The risk of inconsistent copies appears at any size of project.
